--- title: "Einführung in R und Quarto" subtitle: "Vectors" author: "Andreas Haupt" bibliography: IntRo.bib format: revealjs: theme: style.scss css: global.css slideNumber: true fig-align: center editor: source execute: echo: true cache: true message: false warning: false --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(haven) library(dplyr) allbus <- read_dta("C:/Daten/Allbus/2025/ZA9090_v1-0-0.dta") |> select(eastwest, age, sex, gender_m, gender_f, mstat, incc, hhincc, id03, id07) allbus ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5,571 × 10 eastwest age sex gender_m gender_f mstat incc hhincc 1 1 [ALTE BUNDES… 52 1 [MAN… 4 [SEHR… 1 [..] 1 [VER… 15 [200… 23 [500… 2 1 [ALTE BUNDES… 51 2 [FRA… 0 [GAR … 4 [SEHR… 1 [VER… 14 [175… 19 [300… 3 2 [NEUE BUNDES… 32 2 [FRA… 0 [GAR … 4 [SEHR… -99 [ABG… -32 [NIC… -32 [NIC… 4 1 [ALTE BUNDES… 60 2 [FRA… 2 [..] 2 [..] 1 [VER… 7 [750… 9 [100… 5 1 [ALTE BUNDES… 76 2 [FRA… 0 [GAR … 4 [SEHR… 1 [VER… 7 [750… 23 [500… 6 1 [ALTE BUNDES… 21 1 [MAN… 4 [SEHR… 0 [GAR … 5 [LED… -9 [KEI… -9 [KEI… 7 1 [ALTE BUNDES… 29 2 [FRA… 0 [GAR … 4 [SEHR… 5 [LED… 16 [225… 24 [600… 8 1 [ALTE BUNDES… 50 1 [MAN… 3 [..] 0 [GAR … 5 [LED… 17 [250… 19 [300… 9 1 [ALTE BUNDES… 52 2 [FRA… 0 [GAR … 4 [SEHR… -99 [ABG… -32 [NIC… -32 [NIC… 10 1 [ALTE BUNDES… 75 2 [FRA… 0 [GAR … 4 [SEHR… 1 [VER… 21 [400… 23 [500… # ℹ 5,561 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: id03 , id07 ``` ::: ::: ## (atomic) Vector The most fundamental data type in R is a (atomic) **vector**: a sequence/chain/series of information. You can "concatenate" information into a vector by using `c()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Concatenate the sequence 5 4 3 2 1 to a vector, assign it to object x1, and print it. (x1 <- c(5, 4, 3, 2, 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 4 3 2 4 ``` ::: ::: . . . You can access a specific *element* of a vector via it's vector[**index**]: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Print the second element of x1. x1[2] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 ``` ::: ::: . . . If you want to access several elements, you need to supply another vector to the vector's index: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Print the second and fourth element of x1. x1[c(2, 4)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 2 ``` ::: ::: ## {background-image="https://markosun.files.wordpress.com/2015/06/world-leaders-heights-gra-008.jpg"} ## Numeric vectors ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Numeric** vectors are sequences of numbers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x1 # Print x1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 4 3 2 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(x1) # What class of object is x1? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/VectorTypesNum.png){width="70%"} ::: ::: ## **Transform** numeric vectors To transform numeric vectors, you can use ... ... *arithmetic operators* `+ - * / ^`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (x1 <- x1 + 5) # Assign the object X1 plus 5 added to each of its elements to x1. ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 9 8 7 9 ``` ::: ::: . . . ... a myriad of different *functions*.
::: {.note} See Chapter [5 Data transformation](http://r4ds.had.co.nz/transform.html) of @grolemundDataScience2017 for further examples. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (x1 <- log2(x1)) # Assign the logarithm with base 2 of x1 to x1. ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.321928 3.169925 3.000000 2.807355 3.169925 ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {.centered} ::: {.alert} Watch out, R simply overrides existing objects without a warning! ::: ::: . . . Because R is **nested**, you can combine arithmetic operators and several functions in one line. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (x1 <- (x1 - mean(x1)) / sd(x1)) # z-standardize x1. ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.1606991 0.3872282 -0.4774386 -1.4577170 0.3872282 ``` ::: ::: ## {background-image="images/Categorical.jpg"} ## Factor vectors ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/VectorTypesFac.png){width="70%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Factors** are for categorical variables that make a distinction but whose values cannot be compared on a common scale. They are composed of a sequence of categorical *values* (i.e., argument x), and a (ideally comprehensive) list of potential *levels* (i.e., theoretically-possible values). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Concatenate argument "x" to a factor and give it a # comprehensive list "levels" of all potential categories. conti <- factor( x = c("Europe", "Africa", "Africa", "Asia", "S.America"), levels = c("Africa", "Asia", "Australia", "Europe", "N.America", "S.America") ) # Print a frequency table of our new factor vector. table(conti) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` conti Africa Asia Australia Europe N.America S.America 2 1 0 1 0 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Factors instead of labels ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://i.vimeocdn.com/portrait/3399477_300x300){width="80%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.centered} ::: {.alert} R forces you to decide whether a variable is
continuous (numeric) or categorical (factor) ::: ::: - Numeric variables have a scale, such as cm, years, or DKK. Hence there is no need for labels. - Categorical variables, by contrast, have no actual representation in numbers. ::: ::: ## **Recoding** factors ::: {.column width="50%"} Because factors are categorical, they cannot be
*numerically* transformed.
::: {.note} What would be Africa devided by half in comparison to Europe devided by half? :::
If you nevertheless try to numerically transform a factor,
the result is `NA` (i.e., "not available"). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} conti * 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA NA NA NA NA ``` ::: ::: ::: {.centered} ::: {.alert} In R factors need to be handled as fundamentally different from numeric! ::: ::: ::: . . . ::: {.column width="50%"} *Base* R is rather confusing when it comes to factors. We learn to use recode functions from the forcats package, which is part of the tidyverse. ![](https://forcats.tidyverse.org/logo.png){width="50%"} ::: ## Wait, what's a **package**? ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](http://cdn.osxdaily.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/package-file-check.jpg){width="60%"} ::: . . . ::: {.column width="50%"} A **package** is a collection of functions and their documentation (sometimes also data). Some packages are pre-installed as sub-packages of R's *Base* package. In addition, there are, currently, +17,000 (user-written) packages on the *Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN)*. The tidyverse and its forcats package are such user-written packages. You can install any of the +17,000 (user-written) packages using `install.packages("name_of_the_package")`. Please all install the tidyverse package now by typing: `install.packages("tidyverse")` into the *console*. ::: {.note} Do not add the `install.packages()` call to your R Scripts! You will need to install a package only once, and not every time you run your script. If you want to update, use `update.packages()`. ::: ::: ## The **library** ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} Because there are so many user-written packages, they oftentimes contain functions with *conflicting names*. To avoid conflicts, you need to specify for each R session, which packages you want to work with. You do that, by adding the packages to your current R session's **library**. It is good practice to add all packages to the library on the very top of an R script. Please all add the tidyverse to your library by writing the following as the very first line in your R script. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Add tidyverse package to library library(tidyverse) ``` ::: Some tidyverse functions conflict with Base R's Stats package. ::: {.note} You can always address a function from a specific package by initiating it with `package::function()`. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://bucket.trending.com/trending/reddit/2016-12-11/the-incredible-library-at-the-university-of-copenhagen-in-denmark_preview.jpg){width="70%"} ::: ::: ## Back to **recoding** factors ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://forcats.tidyverse.org/logo.png){width="60%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Factors can best be **recoded** with `forcats::fct_recode()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Recode conti to Danish. Watch out: first the new, then the old value... conti <- fct_recode(conti, "Europa" = "Europe", "Afrika" = "Africa", "Asien" = "Asia", "Suedamerika" = "S. America", "Nordamerika" = "N. America", "Australien" = "Australia") # Frequency table of conti. table(conti) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` conti Afrika Asien Australien Europa N.America S.America 2 1 0 1 0 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Back to **recoding** factors ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://forcats.tidyverse.org/logo.png){width="60%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} forcats contains [many more useful functions](https://forcats.tidyverse.org/reference/index.html) to handle factors!
::: {.note} Also check out [Chapter 15 Factors](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/factors.html) of @grolemundDataScience2017. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} conti <- fct_drop(conti) # Drop unused levels. # Frequency table of conti. table(conti) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` conti Afrika Asien Europa S.America 2 1 1 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Reorder factor levels by hand conti <- fct_relevel(conti, "Europa", "Afrika", "Suedamerika", "Asien") # Frequency table of conti. table(conti) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` conti Europa Afrika Asien S.America 1 2 1 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Date vectors ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Dates** are vectors of the Year-Month-Day (and sometimes -Time) format. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Sys.Date() # Tell me the date ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "2026-10-30" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Evaluate the logical statement that # today is smaller (i.e., before) # than the deadline for the exam. Sys.Date() < "2020-05-25" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: Date vectors are complex, because time is not metric $\rightarrow$ advanced R course. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/VectorTypesDate.png){width="70%"} ::: ::: ## Character vectors ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Character**/string vectors are sequences of text. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Concatenate these five strings as one vector # and assign it to object "x2". x2 <- c("This is", "!", "a", "good idea", "really") # Return only the first to third character # of each string-element of x2. (x2 <- str_sub(x2, start = 1, end = 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Thi" "!" "a" "goo" "rea" ``` ::: ::: You can **manipulate** them using string functions and *regular expressions* $\rightarrow$ ::: {.alert} advanced R course (taught by Friedolin Merhout ;) ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/VectorTypesChar.png){width="70%"} ::: ::: ## Logical vectors ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Logical** vectors are sequences of `TRUE` and `FALSE` statements: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x3 <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE) ``` ::: Internally, R uses *logical vectors for case selection*. They are thus very important! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Thi" "!" "a" "goo" "rea" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Print those elements that x3 identifies as TRUE, # but not the FALSE ones. x2[x3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Thi" "a" "goo" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/VectorTypesLogic.png){width="70%"} ::: ::: ## No mixed vectors ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Concacenate the sequence 1-4 to a numeric vector (x4 <- seq(1, 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Replace the third element with the word "test" x4[3] <- "test" x4 # print x4 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "1" "2" "test" "4" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # What type of object is x4? class(x4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Make x4 a numeric vector again as.numeric(x4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 NA 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.centered} ::: {.alert} A (atomic) vector cannot mix types! ::: ::: ![](images/VectorTypesLogic.png){width="70%"} ::: ::: ## **NA**: **N**ot **A**vailable In general, missing values in R are `NA`, impossible values (devision by 0) are `NaN` (Not a Number). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x5 <- c(1, 2, 3, NA, 5, NA, 7) ``` ::: . . . ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} Many functions will not ignore `NA` by default and thus return `NA`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Estimate mean of x5 mean(x5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Estimate mean of x5 ignoring # the NA (i.e., casewise deletion) mean(x5, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.6 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} `is.na()` generates logical vectors that identify missing values. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Which elements are missing? is.na(x5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Which elements are not missing? !is.na(x5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Print only non-missing values of x5 x5[!is.na(x5)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 5 7 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Today's general lessons 1. The most fundamental data type in R is a (atomic) *vector*: a sequence/chain/series of information. Elements of a vector can be addressed via it's *index* `[i]`. We can feed vectors into an index of another vector to address certain elements. 2. There are different classes of vectors: *numeric*, *factor*, *date*, *character*, and *logical* vectors. We can *transform* numeric vectors with arithmetic operators and a myriad of different functions. We can *recode* factor vectors with the `fct_recode()` function. 3. R has no labels. The idea is that numeric variables have a scale (e.g., cm, years, DKK), while categorical variables have no true representation in numbers. 4. R code may be *nested*, that is, you can write functions into functions. More on that later! 5. `NA`: is "Not Available" and thus the code for missing values in R. `NaN` are impossible numeric values. 6. There are no value lables in R. You will need to decide whether a variable is continuous or categorical. 7. R functions are contained in *packages*, which are bundles of functions along with their documentation. To avoid conflicts, you need to add the packages you will use in a certain R session to the *library*. ## Today's (important) functions 1. `install.packages()`: Installs packages from CRAN. 2. `library()`: adds a package to the library for the current session. 3. `c()`: concatenate a sequence to a vector. 4. `factor()`: Make a vector categorical. 5. `fct_recode`: Recode values of a factor. 6. `as.numeric()`: Make a vector numeric. 6. `table()`: simple frequency or cross table. 7. `is.na()`: generate logical vector that identifies missing values. ## Literatur ::: {#refs} :::
